fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title":"A Solar Storm Missing From the Record","body":"Howdie opens with his video on the Carrington event, the solar storm said to have struck in 1859, knocking out telegraph lines worldwide and lighting the skies like an aurora. He relays another researcher's search of old Encyclopaedia Britannica editions back to 1879 that list Carrington the astronomer but never the event, and says people who checked September 1859 newspapers found nothing. His question is why a story that barely surfaces before 2000 is being revived now, and he suggests it is being primed for future talk of power grid failure. Chance hears a self-referential loop with no foundation and wonders whether mass belief helps make such things possible."},{"title":"Painted Curtains and Plato's Cave","body":"When the talk turns to Plato's Cave, Howdie reaches for the history book he is writing alongside his Plato's Cave project. A Last Supper in the main gallery in Nantes sets the table as a twisted square and frames the scene with two curtains pulled aside, and on his first visit to the Sistine Chapel he ignored the ceiling to study walls painted with curtains. He reads both as the theater of Plato's Cave and the veil of Isis, where the task is to open the curtains. Painted curtains add a twist, since parting them would only meet a wall, yet Howdie guesses hours of meditative staring might dissolve them."},{"title":"A Second Relief Behind the First","body":"Howdie describes sitting about an hour and a half in a side room of the seldom visited Temple of Khonsu at Karnak, where guards who knew him from repeat visits left him alone. The wall shimmered like a heat mirage and a different relief appeared, a more feminine scene with different hieroglyphs, for ten or fifteen minutes before the original returned. He concluded the carvings were made holographically in layers reached through one's state of being. Chance links this to defocusing the gaze, wonders whether the artists carved an astral version in dream time, and notes that Disney's Moon Knight gives Khonsu an avatar who sees layers others miss."},{"title":"Tapping the Selves You Might Have Been","body":"Talk of avatars opens onto the multiverse. Howdie says he has experienced himself living other lives, with different jobs and marriages, each a small turn away from this one, and argues a simulation would run many versions to gather experience, though no version of him becomes the Dallas Cowboys quarterback. He suspects some vivid dreams are bleed from those lives. Chance asks whether we could borrow the mastery of a self who spent a lifetime painting, and Howdie runs with it, picturing fixing a car by tapping a self who knows mechanics. Chance's outro adds a reservation: reality is one, so how can a universe hold a multiverse?"},{"title":"Cathedrals, Iron and the Stone Circle Hotspot","body":"Howdie's World's Fair research began on a 2019 trip to Florence studying cathedrals as energy structures. He describes energy drawn down through domes, towers and copper and up from sites built over older temples, meeting and circling the side aisles, with the organ steering it out through rose windows he reads as cymatic patterns and iron balconies drawing it into homes. Chance suggests iron reinforced columns held a constant magnetic field and wonders about mercury engines spinning in octagonal cavities. Howdie adds that in the fifty or sixty Norwegian stone circles he has visited, one spot always runs strongest, and nearly everyone he tests picks the same one."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Howdy Mickoski returns to InnerVerse for his second appearance, and this one covers more ground than the first. The opening thread alone, whether the Carrington Event of 1859 actually happened, or was seeded into history after the year 2000 to prime humanity for a coming grid-down narrative, sets the tone for two hours of careful questioning of what we think we know.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: Topics: the Carrington Event as possibly fabricated history and what it might be conditioning us to expect; the spiritual multiverse as a lived experience, Howdy's direct perception of parallel lives and what that means for how we understand skill, memory, and identity; how a simulation designed for maximum experience would naturally run millions of simultaneous versions of you; free energy architecture and the mercury vortex engine theory, how magnetically resonant cathedrals and iron-threaded buildings may have harvested etheric energy perpetually; Howdy's visit to the Temple of Khonsu at Karnak and what he perceived in the holographic layers above the physical structure; why Moon Knight arriving as a Disney series at this exact moment is stranger than it looks; and the gift economy as a practical alternative to the monetary exchange trap.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Mounds and the Fair Built On Them", "body": "Chance opens the members hour asking about mound building culture after visiting the Cahokia Mounds in Illinois with friends from the audience, where they drove copper earth pipes packed with crystal and resin into the ground. Howdie's first objection is that nobody has excavated deeply enough to prove there was never a structure under the dirt. He then walks through the 1904 St Louis World's Fair, supposedly built after bulldozing twenty or thirty giant mounds across the river, and relays a claim he was told that the real Cahokia site is where the fair actually stood."}, {"title": "Circuit Board Earth and the Older Internet", "body": "From the mounds the talk widens into what Chance calls a circuit board Earth, the grid of roads and cul de sacs visible from above in country that is otherwise empty. He suggests many of those lines were shallow canals, a network of moving water distributing etheric resonance for farming, and raises Chatsworth in the UK, where a drought burned off the vegetation and exposed the imprint of structures that were no longer there. Howdie answers that our internet is a dumbed down copy of something carried in our heritage for tens of thousands of years."}, {"title": "Weighing a Living Heart Against Maat", "body": "A listener question sends them to the weighing of the heart. Howdie rejects the usual title Book of the Dead, arguing the text reads better as becoming light and has nothing to do with a corpse. The heart is weighed against the feather of Maat while Thoth records and Ammit waits, yet the person on the scales is alive and dying only to their ordinary self and worldview. He reads the forty two so called confessions, always phrased as I have not done, as a record of refusing whatever keeps a person inside Plato's cave."}, {"title": "Ptah, Vulcan and the Bound Creator", "body": "Chance asks whether Egypt has a Vulcan figure, a metallurgist artificer answering to the Masonic grand architect, and Howdie points to Ptah, always shown bald, fully human and mummy wrapped, a creator who is himself bound inside his own creation. That opens onto the Cathars, for whom all matter is the work of Rex Mundi. Chance pushes back on what he calls pop culture gnosticism and the body as a prison, arguing that demonizing everything physical also demonizes the feminine. Howdie's caution is blunter, that no Cathars, gnostics or Egyptian priests remain to be asked."}, {"title": "The Dead Internet and the Hidden Layer", "body": "The last stretch belongs to the dead internet. Howdie walks through a search promising over a billion results that quietly ends at page twenty one with two hundred and twenty seven, so either the pages were scrubbed or they survive unfindable because nobody remembers a web address. He could not recover a spiritual site he had relied on for years until its name surfaced on its own. Chance ties this back to the temple relief, a hidden layer sitting behind the one everyone stares at, and to Khonsu as a keeper of what stays out of sight."}]
